lesson.subject: science
lesson.title: The Water Cycle
lesson.subtitle: Evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection, and around again

plan.curriculum: Science 2.0, Earth and space sciences: the water cycle, taught here as the school's Year 5/6 unit (check the level against the school scope and sequence)
plan.shape: example-first with a faded diagram: the loop is new, so the I Do follows one drop before the names are removed
plan.criticalFeature: the same water travels the whole loop; warming lifts it as vapour, cooling turns it back into drops
decisionPoints: the practice round of everyday cases
the hinge: cycle or straight line

studentTools: Printed Water Cycle Scaffold for students who need it
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Show me A, B or C
boardSetup: A blank cycle ring drawn on the board with four empty labels, filled live during the I Do

resources.label: Water Cycle Scaffold
resources.description: Enabling scaffold for the You Do. The four stages are named and pictured; students order them, draw the loop and explain it.
resources.title: The Water Cycle
resources.subtitle: Order the stages, draw the loop, explain why it repeats.

blocks.label: Draw the cycle as a loop. Add arrows to show the water moving.

blocks.heading: Why is it a cycle and not a line?

blocks.tip: Stretch: where in the loop could the water be stored for a long time? Mark it on your drawing.

slides.notes: Open Session 1 of the unit. One line: today we follow one drop of water around a loop that never runs out.

Prep slide. Journals and whiteboards out. Draw the blank cycle ring on the board with four empty labels; it is filled live during the I Do. Print a few Water Cycle Scaffolds for students who need a different entry to the You Do. No earlier session is assumed.

slides.title: Where does rain come from?
slides.prompt: Turn and tell: where does the water in a puddle go on a hot day?

notes.answer: open - it dries up, goes into the air, becomes cloud
beats: POINT to the four pictures.
SAY: Here are four pictures: sun, cloud, rain and sea. They tell one story.
ASK: Where does the water in a puddle go on a hot day?
30 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: it dries up, goes into the air.
SCAN for into the air.
80%+ -> cold call one pair: where does it go next?
Less -> hold up a wet cloth, ask where the water goes, re-ask.
SAY: So the water doesn't disappear. Today we follow where it goes.
trap: saying the water disappears.
Fix: ask if the sun can destroy water, student rethinks.
notes.prep: Launch surfaces the disappears misconception before the model corrects it. Low-coupling, under 5 minutes.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning how water moves and changes as it travels through the water cycle.
successCriteria: I can name the four stages of the water cycle.
I can put the stages in order and say what happens to the water at each one.
I can explain why the water cycle never runs out.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Today we learn how water moves and changes through the water cycle.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: Naming the stages is where we start.
Saying what the water does at each one is our goal today.
notes.prep: SC1 naming is reachable for all; SC2 order and process is the core target; SC3 the never-runs-out explanation is the exit ticket stretch.

slides.meaning: Liquid water warms up and rises into the air as an invisible gas called water vapour.
slides.example: A puddle dries in the sun. The water evaporated.

notes.answer: liquid water warming and rising into the air as water vapour
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Evaporation. Say it with me. E-vap-o-ra-tion.
SAY: Liquid water warms up and rises into the air as an invisible gas.
We call that gas water vapour. You cannot see it, but it is there.
ASK: Is the puddle water gone, or somewhere else?
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: somewhere else, in the air as vapour
trap: saying evaporation makes the water disappear.
Fix: ask what the water turned into, student says vapour in the air.
notes.prep: First of two key words. The word carries the up half of the loop.

slides.meaning: Water vapour cools high in the sky and turns back into tiny drops that make clouds.
slides.example: Drops form on the outside of a cold can. That is condensation.

notes.answer: water vapour cooling and turning back into tiny drops
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Condensation. Say it with me. Con-den-sa-tion.
SAY: High up it is cold. The vapour cools and turns back into tiny drops.
Millions of tiny drops together are a cloud.
ASK: Evaporation goes up. Which way does condensation get us ready to go?
10 sec. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
EXPECT: down, back to drops
trap: swapping evaporation and condensation.
Fix: evaporation up and invisible, condensation cool and drops. Student says both.
notes.prep: Second key word, the turn at the top of the loop. Precipitation and collection are taught inside the diagram, not as extra cards.

slides.title: Follow one drop around the loop
promptLines: I will name each stage and say what the water is doing.
Follow the arrows around the loop.

steps.label: Precipitation
steps.detail: Drops fall as rain, hail or snow

steps.label: Collection
steps.detail: Water gathers in rivers, lakes, sea

notes.answer: up; then evaporation, and around again
beats: POINT to evaporation.
SAY: Let's follow one drop. The sun warms the sea and it rises as vapour.
ASK: Is the vapour going up or down now?
5 sec. Cue: voices off. Point... now.
EXPECT: pointing up
POINT to condensation, then precipitation.
SAY: High up it cools into a cloud drop, then falls as rain.
POINT to collection.
ASK: It gathers in the sea. Which stage comes next?
10 sec. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
EXPECT: evaporation
trap: thinking each stage is new water.
Fix: trace one drop, student re-traces.
notes.stretch: Where could a drop be stored for years?
notes.help: Cover the labels; say rising, cooling, falling, gathering.
notes.prep: The model. Critical feature: the same water travels the whole loop; warming lifts it as vapour, cooling turns it back into drops. The think-aloud follows one drop so the cycle reads as one journey, not four facts. SC2.

slides.title: Which stage turns vapour into cloud?
slides.prompt: Show me A, B or C on your board

options.misconception: places clouds with rising, not with cooling
thinks clouds form from rain, not before it

notes.answer: B - condensation. Vapour cools into drops
beats: SAY: Look at all three stages before you choose.
ASK: Which stage turns vapour into cloud?
20 sec. Cue: Write A, B or C... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: B
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call one B: how do you know?
Less -> hold a cold can, point to the drops forming, name it, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's condensation, because cooling turns the vapour into drops. Tick or fix.
trap: choosing A because clouds are up high.
Fix: ask whether evaporation makes vapour or drops, student re-chooses.
notes.prep: First decision point, on the pair of stages students most often swap. Under 80% means the We Do starts by acting the loop out.

slides.title: Name each stage
promptLines: Use the clues to name stages 1 to 4.
Write the four names in order on your whiteboard.

steps.detail: Drops fall as rain, hail or snow
Water gathers in rivers, lakes, sea

beats: SAY: The names are gone, but the clues are still there.
ASK: Name stages 1 to 4 in order.
60 sec. Partner talk, then Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: which one was hard?
Less -> act it: stand for rising, crouch for falling, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: Tick each name in the right place. Fix any that swapped.
trap: swapping condensation and precipitation.
Fix: ask which one is falling, student re-orders.
notes.stretch: Add a label where water is stored for years.
notes.help: Give the first and last names. Ask for the middle.
notes.prep: Guided practice on the same anchor with the labels faded, not the visual (visual-analysis rule). SC1 and SC2.

slides.title: Say what the water does

rows: Falls as rain, hail or snow
Gathers in rivers, lakes and sea

slides.prompt: Partner A covers the right column. Partner B says it. Swap.

notes.answer: rises as vapour, cools into drops, falls, gathers
beats: POINT to the table.
SAY: Here's what the water does at each stage. Now say it without looking.
ASK: Say what the water does at each stage.
90 sec. Partner check: A covers the right column, B says it, swap.
EXPECT: rises as vapour, cools into drops, falls, gathers
SCAN two pairs per table for cools.
80%+ -> next slide.
Less -> choral read the right column, everyone, together, on three, re-ask.
trap: saying makes clouds without cools.
Fix: ask what happens to the vapour first, student adds cools.
notes.stretch: Say the stages backwards. Does the order still work? Why?
notes.help: Cover the last two rows only.
notes.prep: Oral rehearsal of the process language before writing. The table is the anchor; the cover-and-say routine is the practice.

slides.title: Which stage is this?
slides.pivot: act it: stand for rising, crouch for falling, then ask which stage
slides.followUp: cold call one board: is the water warming or cooling?

items.text: Hail bounces off the school roof.
items.answer: precipitation - the drops fall as hail

items.text: Wet footprints on a hot path fade away.
items.answer: evaporation - the water warms and rises as vapour

items.text: A river carries water back to the sea.
items.answer: collection - the water gathers in the sea

items.text: Your breath makes a little cloud on a cold morning.
items.answer: condensation - the vapour in your breath cools into drops
items.say: Condensation. Your warm breath cools into tiny drops. Tick or fix.

items.answer: precipitation - the water falls as snow

items.text: Rainwater runs down the gutter into a creek.
items.answer: collection - the water gathers and flows

items.text: Fog forms over a lake on a cold night.
items.answer: condensation - the vapour cools into tiny drops near the ground
items.say: Condensation. Fog is a cloud near the ground. Tick or fix.

items.text: A puddle on the oval is gone by lunch.
items.answer: evaporation - the water warms and rises as vapour

say: Everyone writes the stage on their board.
trap: calling breath clouds or fog evaporation.
Fix: ask whether the water is warming or cooling, student rewrites.
notes.stretch: Say whether the water is warming or cooling in each one.
notes.help: Keep the cycle diagram on the board and point from it.
notes.prep: Guided retrieval of the four names on new everyday cases. Breath and fog are the near-misses students call evaporation. SC1 and SC2.

slides.title: Hinge question
slides.technique: Turn and tell, then show me
slides.question: What makes this a cycle and not a straight line?

answers: It collects, then evaporates again. The loop repeats.

notes.answer: the water collects, then evaporates again - the loop repeats
beats: SAY: Here's a big question. Think about the arrow back to evaporation.
ASK: What makes this a cycle and not a straight line?
30 sec. Turn and tell, then Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: it goes around again, it repeats.
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: does Earth ever run out of water?
Less -> trace the loop twice, ask where it ends, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It collects, then evaporates again. Same water, around and around.
trap: saying it stops after the rain.
Fix: point to collection, ask what the sun does next.
notes.prep: The hinge of the session and the structure of the exit ticket's second question. SC3.

slides.title: Show what you know in your journal
slides.task: Draw the water cycle as a loop. Label all four stages and add arrows.
steps: Draw the loop with four stages
Add arrows to show the water moving
Write one sentence: why is it a cycle?

notes.answer: a loop with four labels and arrows, plus one sentence about repeating
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Now draw your own diagram: a loop, four labels, arrows and one sentence.
SAY: Draw, arrow, write. Say the steps with me. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Look for arrows pointing the same way and the loop closing.
TIME 12 minutes. Early finishers add where water is stored for years.
trap: four boxes in a line with no return arrow.
Fix: ask where the water goes after collection, student draws the return.
notes.stretch: Add where water is stored for years and how it rejoins.
notes.help: Water Cycle Scaffold: stages pictured, first one named. Order and draw.
notes.prep: Independent application with the same loop as the slides. The journal drawing is the evidence for SC2; the sentence for SC3.

slides.extendedTask: draw and label the water cycle as a loop, with one sentence on why it repeats

slides.title: Before you go
questions: Wet washing dries on the line. Which stage is this, and what does the water do?
Could that same water fall as rain on our school one day? Explain how.

notes.answer: evaporation, rises as vapour; yes, it goes around the loop again
beats: SAY: Two new questions for your whiteboard, about washing on the line.
ASK: Answer both questions on your board.
180 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: evaporation, it rises as vapour; yes, it goes around the loop
RECORD who names the stage and what happens,
and who explains the loop. Two lists for tomorrow.
trap: naming evaporation but not what the water does.
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence on a context not used earlier in the session: question 1 is SC2, question 2 is SC3. Tomorrow groups on question 1.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Tell your partner the four stages in order, from memory, and where the loop starts again.
slides.selfAssessment: Traffic light: green, orange or red on your whiteboard

notes.answer: open - listen for collection leading back to evaporation
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: Traffic light: how well can you explain the whole loop?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: green, orange or red
RECORD each red beside the exit board.
A green with no loop in the exit answer matters most.
ASK: Tell your partner the four stages in order, and where the loop starts again.
30 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection, then evaporation
notes.prep: Self-assessment against the criteria, read beside the exit evidence. Tomorrow's grouping comes from both. SC2.
